comparison: more/most — *more escalating* is rare; the word already means rising

senses.gloss: Getting bigger, worse or more serious step by step.
examples: Families are struggling with *escalating* rents.
The two countries are locked in an *escalating* trade war.
Violence in the region is *escalating*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *escapist fiction*, not *the movie was escapist* in careful writing
contrast: *An escapist* is also a noun — a person who avoids real life.

senses.gloss: Offering a pleasant break from real life and its problems.
examples: She reads *escapist* novels on the beach.
It's pure *escapist* entertainment, and that's the point.
The studio built its name on big, loud, *escapist* movies.

senses.gloss: Understood by only a small group with special knowledge.
examples: The paper is full of *esoteric* mathematical notation.
His interests are pretty *esoteric* — medieval bookbinding, mostly.
The second half of the lecture was even more *esoteric* than the first.

senses.gloss: Existing for a long time and generally accepted or respected.
examples: This is an *established* law firm with offices in three cities.
It is an *established* fact that the drug lowers blood pressure.
She is far more *established* now than she was ten years ago.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *our esteemed guest*
contrast: Formal and often a little ironic in speech: *my esteemed colleague* can be a dig.

senses.gloss: Greatly respected and admired.
examples: Please welcome our *esteemed* guest from Tokyo.
He studied under an *esteemed* professor of physics.
She is the *most esteemed* judge on the panel.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the estimated cost*

senses.gloss: Calculated roughly, not counted exactly.
examples: The *estimated* cost of the repair is $1,200.
An *estimated* 40,000 people attended the concert.
Your *estimated* arrival time is 6:15 p.m.

senses.gloss: No longer friendly or in contact with a family member or partner.
examples: He lives with his *estranged* wife's parents.
She has been *estranged* from her father for years.
The brothers grew more *estranged* after the funeral.

comparison: not gradable — something either lasts forever or does not

senses.gloss: Lasting forever, with no beginning and no end.
examples: They believe in *eternal* life.
An *eternal* flame burns at the memorial.
Nothing in this world is *eternal*.

senses.gloss: Seeming to go on and on, in an annoying way.
examples: I'm tired of your *eternal* complaining.
There is the *eternal* question of who pays for it.

senses.gloss: Light, delicate and beautiful in a way that seems not of this world.
examples: The singer has an *ethereal* voice.
Morning fog gave the lake an *ethereal* look.
Her paintings are even more *ethereal* in person.

senses.gloss: Morally right, or behaving according to moral rules.
examples: It isn't *ethical* to read someone else's mail.
They promise *ethical* treatment of the animals.
This company is far *more ethical* than its competitors.

senses.gloss: Having to do with questions of right and wrong.
examples: The study raises serious *ethical* questions.
Every doctor here signs an *ethical* code.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an ethnic minority*
contrast: Of people and culture, not of a country: a citizen of Russia may be *ethnic* Korean.

senses.gloss: Having to do with a group that shares a culture, language or origin.
examples: The country has more than a hundred *ethnic* groups.
*Ethnic* tension in the region goes back centuries.
She grew up in an *ethnic* neighborhood on the South Side.

senses.gloss: Using a mild or vague word in place of a blunt one.
examples: "Letting people go" is a *euphemistic* way of saying "firing them."
The report is written in *euphemistic* corporate language.
His answer was *euphemistic* and told us nothing.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing very great happiness and excitement.
examples: The fans were *euphoric* after the win.
A *euphoric* crowd filled the square.
She felt *euphoric* for about a day, and then the work began.

contrast: Capitalized as a noun for the movement: *Evangelicals voted in large numbers*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the Protestant churches that stress the Bible and personal conversion.
examples: She was raised in an *evangelical* church in Texas.
*Evangelical* voters were a large part of the turnout.

senses.gloss: Trying eagerly to convince other people of a belief.
examples: He is *evangelical* about cold showers.
The company has an almost *evangelical* faith in its own product.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *evaporated milk*
contrast: *Evaporated milk* is unsweetened; *condensed milk* is sweet — a common mix-up in recipes.

senses.gloss: Made thicker by having most of the water removed.
examples: The recipe calls for a can of *evaporated* milk.
Stir the *evaporated* milk into the pumpkin mixture.
You can substitute cream for *evaporated* milk in a pinch.

senses.gloss: Avoiding a direct answer.
examples: The witness gave *evasive* answers all morning.
He was *evasive* about where the money came from.
She got *more evasive* the longer we talked.

senses.gloss: Meant to get out of the way of danger.
examples: The pilot took *evasive* action.
The deer made an *evasive* jump into the trees.

contrast: *Even* is also a very common adverb: *even better*, *even if*. That is not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Flat, level and smooth.
examples: Find an *even* surface for the tripod.
The new concrete is much *more even* than the old walkway.

senses.gloss: Equal in number, amount or score, so that nobody owes anything.
examples: Split the check into *even* shares.
You bought lunch, so now we're *even*.

senses.gloss: Of a number, able to be divided by two.
examples: Houses with *even* numbers are on this side of the street.
Two, four and six are *even* numbers.

senses.gloss: Steady and calm, without sudden changes.
examples: She answered in an *even* voice.
Keep the oven at an *even* temperature.

senses.gloss: Treating everyone fairly and in the same way.
examples: The judge is known for her *even-handed* rulings.
He was *even-handed* with both of his children.
This is the *most even-handed* account of the war I have read.

senses.gloss: Calm by nature and not easily made angry.
examples: He is an *even-tempered* man who rarely raises his voice.
Golden retrievers are usually *even-tempered*.
She is *more even-tempered* than anyone else on the team.

senses.gloss: Full of interesting or important things happening.
examples: We had an *eventful* week in Chicago.
Her life has been *eventful*, to say the least.
That was the *most eventful* game of the season.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the ever-changing rules*

senses.gloss: Always becoming different, never staying the same.
examples: Teachers face an *ever-changing* set of state requirements.
The *ever-changing* light on the water is what drew him to paint here.
It is hard to keep up with the *ever-changing* tax code.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the ever-present risk*

senses.gloss: Always there, and never going away.
examples: Wildfire is an *ever-present* danger in this valley.
He walked in with his *ever-present* coffee cup.
There is the *ever-present* question of who will pay.

contrast: *An evergreen* is also a noun — the tree itself: *We planted three evergreens*.

senses.gloss: Of a tree or bush, keeping its green leaves all year.
examples: Pines and firs are *evergreen*.
A row of *evergreen* shrubs hides the fence.

senses.gloss: Staying useful or popular no matter how much time passes.
examples: "How to save for retirement" is *evergreen* content.
It's an *evergreen* question in American politics.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *everlasting life*

senses.gloss: Lasting forever, or seeming to.
examples: The hymn promises *everlasting* life.
He has my *everlasting* gratitude.
I'm tired of their *everlasting* arguments about money.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *everyday life*
contrast: One word before a noun; two words as a time phrase: *everyday problems* but *I see him every day*.

senses.gloss: Ordinary and happening as part of normal life.
examples: The book is about the *everyday* lives of factory workers.
These are *everyday* dishes, not the good china.
Spanish is her *everyday* language at home.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *evidence-based medicine*

senses.gloss: Built on research and proof rather than on opinion or habit.
examples: The clinic uses only *evidence-based* treatments.
She wants *evidence-based* policy, not guesswork.
The district adopted an *evidence-based* reading program.

comparison: -er/-est or more/most — *eviler* or *more evil*, *evilest* or *most evil*
contrast: *Evil* is also a noun: *the problem of evil*, *a necessary evil*.

senses.gloss: Deeply bad in a moral way, and wanting to harm others.
examples: He plays the *evil* wizard in the new movie.
No one is born *evil*.
She is the *most evil* character in the whole series.

senses.gloss: Very unpleasant, especially to the nose.
examples: An *evil* smell came from the basement.
He gave me an *evil* look and walked out.

senses.gloss: Bringing strong pictures, memories or feelings to mind.
examples: The book has an *evocative* description of a Brooklyn summer.
The music is *evocative* of the 1970s.
His photographs are *more evocative* than any of the text.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *evolutionary biology*
contrast: In business writing it means *gradual*, the opposite of *revolutionary*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the slow development of living things over time.
examples: She teaches *evolutionary* biology at Michigan.
Color vision gave early primates an *evolutionary* advantage.

senses.gloss: Happening by small steps rather than all at once.
examples: The new phone is *evolutionary*, not revolutionary.
They favor an *evolutionary* approach to reform.

contrast: *Exact* is also a formal verb — *to exact a price*. And *exacting* means "demanding," not "precise."

senses.gloss: Completely correct and with no error in the details.
examples: What were his *exact* words?
I need the *exact* measurements before I cut the wood.
Her figures are *more exact* than the ones in the first report.

contrast: Not "precise." An *exacting* boss demands a lot; an *exact* figure is correct to the decimal.

senses.gloss: Demanding a great deal of care, effort or skill.
examples: Watchmaking is *exacting* work.
She is an *exacting* editor who questions every comma.
The standards here are *more exacting* than at my last job.

senses.gloss: Made to seem larger, better or worse than it really is.
examples: Reports of the damage were *exaggerated*.
He has an *exaggerated* idea of his own importance.
The second telling was even *more exaggerated* than the first.

senses.gloss: Larger than normal on purpose, for effect.
examples: The actor gave an *exaggerated* bow.
The jacket has *exaggerated* shoulders.

senses.gloss: Very high in rank or importance.
examples: He rose to the *exalted* position of chief justice.
From her *exalted* seat on the board, she rarely met a customer.
Few writers reach such an *exalted* place in the language.

senses.gloss: Noble and full of high feeling.
examples: The speech was written in an *exalted* style.
She left the concert in an *exalted* mood.

contrast: *-ed* is the person who feels it; *-ing* is what causes it: *I was exasperated by his exasperating questions*.

senses.gloss: Very annoyed, especially after trying to be patient for a long time.
examples: She let out an *exasperated* sigh.
I'm *exasperated* with the whole process.
By the fourth phone call he was *more exasperated* than angry.

senses.gloss: Making someone very annoyed.
examples: Waiting on hold for an hour is *exasperating*.
He has an *exasperating* habit of answering a question with a question.
The form is *more exasperating* than the tax itself.

senses.gloss: Much better than usual.
examples: The service at that restaurant is *exceptional*.
She is an *exceptional* student.
This year's crop was the *most exceptional* in a decade.

senses.gloss: Unusual, and not what normally happens.
examples: We make refunds only in *exceptional* cases.
The delay was due to *exceptional* weather.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *excess baggage*
contrast: *Excess* names the extra amount itself (*excess weight*); *excessive* judges it as too much (*excessive force*).

senses.gloss: More than the amount that is allowed or needed.
examples: The airline charges $75 for *excess* baggage.
Drain off any *excess* fat before adding the onions.
You can roll *excess* contributions into next year.

contrast: *Excessive* always judges the amount as too much; *excess* only says there is extra.

senses.gloss: Much more than is reasonable or acceptable.
examples: The officer was fired for *excessive* force.
Ten dollars for a coffee seems *excessive*.
Their spending grew *more excessive* every year.

senses.gloss: Able to be traded for something else.
examples: Sale items are not *exchangeable*.
The points are *exchangeable* for flights or hotel nights.
Keep the receipt, or the gift won't be *exchangeable*.

senses.gloss: Becoming excited or upset very easily.
examples: The puppy is friendly but *excitable*.
He's an *excitable* kid who can't sit still.
She gets *more excitable* the closer we get to a deadline.

contrast: *An exclusive* is also a noun in journalism — a story only one outlet has.

senses.gloss: Available to one person or group and to nobody else.
examples: The magazine has an *exclusive* interview with the director.
This offer is *exclusive* to members.

senses.gloss: Expensive, and open only to people the owners choose.
examples: They joined an *exclusive* country club.
It's the *most exclusive* address in the city.

senses.gloss: Unable to be true or to happen at the same time as something else.
examples: The two goals are not mutually *exclusive*.
These categories are *exclusive*, so pick only one.

contrast: Often a joke about boredom rather than pain: *an excruciating three-hour meeting*.

senses.gloss: Causing extreme pain.
examples: The pain in his back was *excruciating*.
She suffered an *excruciating* migraine for two days.

senses.gloss: Extremely boring, embarrassing or hard to sit through.
examples: The wedding toast was *excruciating*.
He described every detail in *excruciating* detail.

senses.gloss: Not too bad to be forgiven.
examples: A first mistake is *excusable*.
Being late once is *excusable*; being late every day is not.
Her sharp answer was *more excusable* than it sounded, given the week she'd had.

contrast: *An executable* is also a noun in computing — the program file itself.

senses.gloss: Of a computer file, able to be run as a program.
examples: Don't open *executable* attachments from strangers.
The installer ships as a single *executable* file.
Make the script *executable* before you run it.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an executive decision*
contrast: *An executive* is far more common as a noun — a senior manager: *She's a bank executive*.

senses.gloss: Having the power to run an organization and make decisions.
examples: The president signed an *executive* order.
I made an *executive* decision and ordered pizza for everyone.
She sits on the *executive* committee.

senses.gloss: So good that it should serve as a model for others.
examples: His military service was *exemplary*.
She keeps an *exemplary* set of records.
Of all the applications, hers was the *most exemplary*.

senses.gloss: Of a punishment, severe, so as to warn other people.
examples: The jury awarded *exemplary* damages.
The court wanted an *exemplary* sentence in this case.

senses.gloss: Making you feel very happy, awake and full of energy.
examples: The ride down the mountain was *exhilarating*.
There's something *exhilarating* about a cold morning swim.
Her first week in New York was the *most exhilarating* of her life.

senses.gloss: Forced to live away from your own country.
examples: The *exiled* king settled in Portugal.
She was *exiled* from her homeland at nineteen.
*Exiled* writers kept the language alive abroad.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an existential threat*

senses.gloss: Threatening the very existence of something.
examples: Climate change is an *existential* threat to the islands.
The lawsuit is an *existential* risk for the company.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the meaning and purpose of human life.
examples: He's having an *existential* crisis at forty.
The novel asks *existential* questions about free will.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the existing rules*
contrast: Use *existing* for what is already there, *existent* almost never — the common word is its opposite, *nonexistent*.

senses.gloss: Present now, before any change is made.
examples: The *existing* law already covers this.
We'll connect the new wing to the *existing* building.
*Existing* customers keep their old rate.

contrast: *Exonerated* means cleared of blame; *acquitted* only means the jury did not convict.

senses.gloss: Officially cleared of blame for something.
examples: He was fully *exonerated* after new evidence appeared.
The *exonerated* men spent nineteen years in prison.
She was *exonerated* of any wrongdoing by the review board.

contrast: Almost always about money — prices, rent, fees — not about size or effort.

senses.gloss: Of a price or charge, far too high.
examples: They charge *exorbitant* fees for a simple wire transfer.
Rent downtown is *exorbitant*.
The bar's prices are *more exorbitant* than the restaurant's.

senses.gloss: From a distant country, and unusual or exciting because of that.
examples: The market sells *exotic* fruit you can't find in stores.
They keep *exotic* pets — a python and two parrots.
Hawaii sounded *exotic* to a kid from Ohio.

senses.gloss: Strikingly unusual or striking in appearance.
examples: She has an *exotic* taste in hats.
The *most exotic* thing on the menu was the octopus.

senses.gloss: Able to be made larger.
examples: The suitcase has an *expandable* section for the trip home.
Storage is *expandable* up to two terabytes.
We bought an *expandable* dining table.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *expansionist policies*
contrast: *An expansionist* is also a noun — a person who favors such a policy.

senses.gloss: Aiming to make a country's or company's territory or power larger.
examples: The empire pursued *expansionist* policies for a century.
Neighbors watched his *expansionist* ambitions with alarm.
The chain's *expansionist* strategy added 300 stores in two years.

senses.gloss: Covering a wide area, or wide in scope.
examples: The house has an *expansive* view of the bay.
She gave an *expansive* answer that covered the whole century.

senses.gloss: Friendly, talkative and willing to say a lot.
examples: After a glass of wine he became *expansive*.
The coach was *more expansive* with reporters than usual.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the expatriate community*
contrast: Usually a noun, and usually shortened: *She's an expat in Lisbon*. Not the same as *immigrant*, though the difference is mostly about who is speaking.

senses.gloss: Living outside your own country, usually for work.
examples: There's a large *expatriate* community in Dubai.
The school serves *expatriate* families.
He writes for an *expatriate* newspaper in Paris.

senses.gloss: Looking as if you are waiting for something good to happen.
examples: The dog sat by the door with an *expectant* look.
An *expectant* hush fell over the theater.
The crowd grew *more expectant* as the hour approached.

senses.gloss: Pregnant, or about to become a parent.
examples: The class is for *expectant* mothers.
*Expectant* fathers are welcome too.

senses.gloss: Thought likely to happen or to arrive.
examples: The *expected* delivery date is Friday.
His reaction was entirely *expected*.
Turnout was lower than *expected*.

contrast: Not "fast." *Expedient* means useful right now, often at the cost of what is right — that is *expeditious*.

senses.gloss: Useful or convenient in a situation, though perhaps not honest or fair.
examples: It was politically *expedient* to blame the previous administration.
They took the *expedient* route and settled out of court.
Firing him would be *more expedient* than fixing the process.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *expedited shipping*

senses.gloss: Handled faster than by the normal process.
examples: Pay $20 extra for *expedited* shipping.
She applied for *expedited* passport service.
The court granted an *expedited* review of the case.

contrast: Formal, and about speed. *Expedient* is about convenience, not speed — do not swap them.

senses.gloss: Done quickly and efficiently.
examples: We ask for an *expeditious* response to the complaint.
Mailing the form is the *most expeditious* way to do it.
Their handling of the recall was *expeditious*.

senses.gloss: Able to be given up or used up, because it is not essential.
examples: The workers felt *expendable*.
Gloves and masks are treated as *expendable* supplies.
In a budget cut, training is the first *expendable* item.

contrast: Things are *expensive*; people who spend a lot are *extravagant*. And a price is *high*, not *expensive*.

senses.gloss: Costing a lot of money.
examples: That's an *expensive* car for a first job.
Dinner downtown is *expensive*.
The repair turned out to be *more expensive* than the car was worth.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *experiential learning*

senses.gloss: Based on doing something rather than on reading or hearing about it.
examples: The program is built around *experiential* learning.
She studies the *experiential* side of memory.
The museum's new wing is fully *experiential*.

comparison: more/most — *more experimental*, *most experimental* (of art and music)

senses.gloss: Still being tested, and not yet proven or approved.
examples: He enrolled in a trial of an *experimental* drug.
The treatment is still *experimental*.

senses.gloss: Using new and unusual methods, especially in art.
examples: She writes *experimental* poetry.
Their second album is *more experimental* than the first.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *expert advice*
takes: *at* or *in* + noun or *-ing* (mainly with the noun: *an expert at fixing things*)
contrast: *An expert* is far more common as a noun. As an adjective it goes before the noun; say *she is an expert on birds*, not *she is expert*.

senses.gloss: Having or showing great skill and knowledge.
examples: We got *expert* advice from a tax attorney.
The piece was restored by *expert* hands.
He is the *most expert* witness they could find.

contrast: For food Americans say *expired* or *out of date*, never *overdue* — that is for library books and bills.

senses.gloss: No longer valid, because the date on it has passed.
examples: They wouldn't accept my *expired* driver's license.
Throw out the *expired* medication.
Your coupon is *expired*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an explanatory note*
contrast: Note the spelling: *explain* loses its *i* — *explanatory*, *explanation*.

senses.gloss: Meant to make something clearer or easier to understand.
examples: See the *explanatory* note at the bottom of the page.
The manual comes with *explanatory* diagrams.
A short *explanatory* video walks you through the form.

senses.gloss: Said clearly and in detail, leaving no room for doubt.
examples: He gave *explicit* instructions not to be disturbed.
She was *explicit* about what she wanted.
Let me be *more explicit*: the answer is no.

senses.gloss: Showing sex or violence openly.
examples: The album carries an *explicit* lyrics warning.
Some scenes are sexually *explicit*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the exploding population*

senses.gloss: Blowing apart with great force.
examples: The movie ends with an *exploding* helicopter.
*Exploding* fireworks lit up the harbor.

senses.gloss: Growing very fast in number or size.
examples: The city is struggling with an *exploding* population.
*Exploding* demand caught the factory off guard.

senses.gloss: Treating people unfairly in order to profit from them.
examples: The report describes *exploitative* labor practices.
Those interest rates are plainly *exploitative*.
The second contract was even *more exploitative* than the first.

senses.gloss: Used unfairly for someone else's profit.
examples: *Exploited* farm workers often have no legal protection.
Interns felt *exploited* and quit.
She writes about *exploited* garment workers in Los Angeles.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *exploratory talks*

senses.gloss: Done in order to find out more, before anything is decided.
examples: The two sides held *exploratory* talks in Geneva.
The surgeon ordered *exploratory* surgery.
She formed an *exploratory* committee for a Senate run.

contrast: *Explosives* is also a plural noun — the material itself.

senses.gloss: Able to blow up.
examples: Dogs are trained to sniff out *explosive* material.
The gas is highly *explosive*.

senses.gloss: Likely to cause sudden anger, argument or trouble.
examples: The testimony was *explosive*.
Race and money are the *most explosive* topics on the council.

senses.gloss: Sudden, fast and powerful.
examples: The company saw *explosive* growth in its first year.
He's an *explosive* runner off the line.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *exponential growth*
contrast: In math it is exact; in the newspaper it just means "very fast."

senses.gloss: Growing faster and faster, by a larger amount each time.
examples: The chart shows *exponential* growth in users.
Costs rose at an *exponential* rate.
There's been an *exponential* increase in applications.

senses.gloss: Not covered or protected from weather, danger or view.
examples: The cabin sits on an *exposed* ridge.
Don't leave *exposed* wires where kids can reach them.
The north side of the house is *more exposed* to wind.

senses.gloss: Put in contact with something harmful.
examples: Workers were *exposed* to asbestos for years.
Anyone *exposed* to the virus should stay home.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an express train*
contrast: *Express* is also a common verb (*express an opinion*) and a noun (*take the express*). The adjective only goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: Fast, and stopping at few places or handled ahead of the rest.
examples: Take the *express* train to Penn Station.
Ten items or fewer in the *express* lane.
Send it *express* mail if it has to be there Monday.

senses.gloss: Stated clearly and on purpose.
examples: He came for the *express* purpose of apologizing.
You need her *express* permission in writing.

senses.gloss: Showing no feeling on the face or in the voice.
examples: Her face stayed *expressionless* through the whole verdict.
He answered in a flat, *expressionless* voice.
The guard was completely *expressionless*.

senses.gloss: Showing thoughts and feelings clearly.
examples: The baby has big, *expressive* eyes.
His playing is technically fine but not very *expressive*.
She is *more expressive* in her second language than in her first.

senses.gloss: Extremely beautiful and delicately made.
examples: She wore an *exquisite* silk dress.
The carving on the door is *exquisite*.
It was the *most exquisite* meal we had all year.

senses.gloss: Of a feeling, very strong and finely felt.
examples: He has an *exquisite* sense of timing.
Waiting for the results was *exquisite* torture.

contrast: Not *extinct*, its near-opposite: *extant* species are the ones still alive.

senses.gloss: Still existing, especially after a long time.
examples: Only three *extant* copies of the map are known.
The oldest *extant* building in town dates to 1789.
Few of his letters are still *extant*.

contrast: Also spelled *extendible*, but *extendable* is the usual American form.

senses.gloss: Able to be made longer in size or in time.
examples: The ladder is *extendable* to twenty feet.
The lease is *extendable* for another two years.
It comes with an *extendable* handle.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an extended stay*
contrast: *Extended family* means aunts, cousins and grandparents — not a big family.

senses.gloss: Longer than usual or than planned.
examples: He took an *extended* leave after the surgery.
The store has *extended* hours during the holidays.

senses.gloss: Including more than the usual core.
examples: Her *extended* family gathers every Thanksgiving.
The DVD has an *extended* version with twenty more minutes.

contrast: *Extensive* is about how much ground it covers; *intensive* is about how concentrated the effort is.

senses.gloss: Covering a large area or a lot of material.
examples: She has *extensive* experience in public health.
The library's collection is *extensive*.
The damage was *more extensive* than the first reports suggested.

position: attributive only — before a noun, almost always *circumstances*
contrast: It lives in one phrase: *extenuating circumstances*. You will rarely meet it anywhere else.

senses.gloss: Making an offense seem less serious by explaining why it happened.
examples: The judge found *extenuating* circumstances and reduced the sentence.
We can waive the fee if there are *extenuating* circumstances.
There were *extenuating* factors the report never mentioned.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *exterior walls*
contrast: *Exterior* is the outside surface of a thing (a house, a car); *external* is the wider word for anything outside (*external pressure*, *external hard drive*).

senses.gloss: On or forming the outside of something, especially a building.
examples: The *exterior* walls need paint.
Use *exterior* latex for the trim.
They shot the *exterior* scenes in Toronto.

senses.gloss: On the outside, or coming from outside.
examples: The label says "for *external* use only."
I back everything up to an *external* drive.

senses.gloss: Belonging to something outside the group or organization.
examples: The board hired an *external* auditor.
The pressure was *external*, not from anyone on the team.

comparison: not gradable — a species either is or isn't
contrast: *Extinct* (died out) and *extinguished* (put out, of a fire) come from the same root but are not interchangeable.

senses.gloss: No longer existing, of a species or a way of life.
examples: The passenger pigeon has been *extinct* since 1914.
Several frog species have gone *extinct* in the last decade.
Pay phones are all but *extinct*.

senses.gloss: Of a volcano, no longer active and not expected to erupt again.
examples: The island sits on an *extinct* volcano.
Geologists say the crater is *extinct*, not dormant.

senses.gloss: Of a price or rate, so high that it feels like robbery.
examples: The airport charges *extortionate* parking rates.
Payday lenders charge *extortionate* interest.
Their fee is *more extortionate* than anything I've seen.

contrast: *Extra* is also an adverb (*extra large*, *extra carefully*) and a noun (*an extra* in a movie). Note *an extra chair*, never *a extra chair*.

senses.gloss: More than the usual or expected number or amount.
examples: Bring an *extra* pair of socks.
Guacamole is *extra*.
She worked *extra* hours all through December.

senses.gloss: Bigger than the large size.
examples: Do you have this shirt in *extra-large*?
He ordered an *extra-large* pizza for four people.
The recipe calls for two *extra-large* eggs.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *extracurricular activities*
contrast: Jokingly used for an affair: *his extracurricular activities*.

senses.gloss: Done at school but outside regular classes.
examples: Colleges look at *extracurricular* activities too.
Band and debate are her main *extracurricular* interests.
Budget cuts hit the *extracurricular* programs first.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an extramarital affair*

senses.gloss: Happening outside a marriage, with someone who is not your husband or wife.
examples: He admitted to an *extramarital* affair.
The book studies *extramarital* relationships across cultures.
Rumors of an *extramarital* romance ended his campaign.

ru: посторонний, лишний, не относящийся к делу

senses.gloss: Not connected with what is being dealt with, and therefore unnecessary.
examples: Cut the *extraneous* detail from the introduction.
That argument is *extraneous* to the case.
*Extraneous* noise ruined the recording.

contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the *a* of *extra* almost disappears: ik-STROR-duh-ner-ee, not "extra-ordinary."

senses.gloss: Far beyond what is usual, in a way that surprises or impresses.
examples: She has an *extraordinary* memory for names.
What he did that night was *extraordinary*.
It was the *most extraordinary* thing I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Arranged for a special purpose, outside the normal schedule.
examples: The board called an *extraordinary* meeting.
The envoy is an ambassador *extraordinary*.

position: attributive only — before a noun, nearly always *perception*

senses.gloss: Coming from outside the five normal senses.
examples: The lab tested claims of *extrasensory* perception.
She says she has some kind of *extrasensory* ability.
There is no solid evidence for *extrasensory* powers.

contrast: Also a noun, shortened to *ET*: *the search for extraterrestrials*.

senses.gloss: Coming from, or existing, outside the earth.
examples: They scan the sky for *extraterrestrial* signals.
No *extraterrestrial* life has ever been found.
The rock turned out to be *extraterrestrial* in origin.

contrast: *Extremes* is also a noun: *go to extremes*, *the extremes of the desert*.

senses.gloss: Very great in degree, far beyond the normal.
examples: He was in *extreme* pain.
Use it only in an *extreme* emergency.
This winter was *more extreme* than any in living memory.

senses.gloss: Of opinions, far from what most people think, and often dangerous.
examples: He holds *extreme* political views.
That's an *extreme* position, even for him.

senses.gloss: Of sports, dangerous and exciting.
examples: She's into *extreme* sports — base jumping, mostly.
The channel shows *extreme* skiing all winter.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *extremist groups*
contrast: *An extremist* is also a noun, and the commoner use: *the group was founded by extremists*.

senses.gloss: Holding political or religious views far outside the mainstream, often with violence.
examples: The site was taken down for hosting *extremist* content.
He was drawn into an *extremist* group online.
*Extremist* violence rose sharply that year.
